q: What defines Gothic architecture?
n: Gothic architecture is defined by pointed arches, ribbed vaults, flying buttresses and rich sculptural and stained-glass ornament. Semicircular arches are Romanesque. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Gothic architecture.

q: Which of the following is true about Gothic architecture?
n: Gothic churches are roofed with stone rib vaults under timber roofs, not domes. Domes belong to Byzantine and Renaissance work, and Gothic arches are pointed, not semicircular. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: Flying buttresses are typical of which style?
n: Flying buttresses are typical of Gothic architecture. They carry the vault thrust over the aisles to outer piers, which frees the walls for windows. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: Which style is referred to as the architecture of geometry due to its strong emphasis on proportion and symmetry?
n: Gothic design was governed by geometry. Masons laid out plans, elevations and tracery with compass-and-square constructions (ad quadratum, ad triangulum). Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Gothic architecture; Frankl, Gothic Architecture.

q: In architecture, Gothic art was considered the most ___ of its time.
n: Gothic architecture is often described as the most intellectual art of its age. It was linked to scholastic philosophy, its structure a rational system of balanced forces. Source: Panofsky, Gothic Architecture and Scholasticism.

q: In Gothic architecture, which English style is considered closest to the French style?
n: English Decorated Gothic (about 1290–1350), with its elaborate geometric and curvilinear tracery, is closest to French Rayonnant Gothic. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: What was the most common building stone of French Gothic?
n: French Gothic cathedrals were built mainly of local limestone, plentiful in the Paris Basin and northern France and easily carved. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Gothic architecture.

q: Which description was historically attached to Gothic architecture by its critics?
n: Renaissance critics such as Vasari called medieval architecture "Gothic," meaning rude and barbaric after the Goths, in contrast to the classical revival. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Gothic architecture.

q: In French, "l'architecture ogivale" refers to:
n: "L'architecture ogivale" is a 19th-century French name for Gothic architecture, from ogive (the pointed arch or diagonal rib). Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Gothic architecture; Ching.

q: Which style is famous for gargoyles?
n: Gargoyles, carved stone spouts that throw rainwater clear of the walls, are typical of Gothic cathedrals such as Notre-Dame de Paris. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: What architectural innovation was introduced in Gothic walls?
n: Because flying buttresses took the vault loads, Gothic walls between piers could be opened into much larger expanses of glass. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Gothic architecture.

q: What architectural feature became possible in Gothic cathedrals due to new structural support methods?
n: The new Gothic support system of rib vaults and flying buttresses made it possible to fill the walls with many large windows. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Gothic architecture.

q: Which style reached new heights in verticality?
n: Gothic architecture pushed verticality further than any earlier style, with tall naves (Beauvais about 48 m) and spires, using pointed arches and buttressing. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Gothic architecture.

q: What is a continuous row of arches called?
n: An arcade is a continuous row of arches carried on columns or piers. A colonnade is a row of columns carrying an entablature. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: What is the upper wall with windows rising above an adjacent roof?
n: The clerestory is the upper wall of the nave, pierced with windows, that rises above the aisle roofs to admit light. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: What decorative open-timber roof truss of English Gothic uses short brackets projecting from the wall?
n: A hammerbeam roof uses short horizontal brackets (hammer beams) projecting from the wall tops to carry arched braces, letting the roof span wide halls. Westminster Hall (1390s) is the classic example. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture; UK Parliament (Westminster Hall).

q: Which Marian pilgrimage cathedral is known for its three west-front portals (the Royal Portal)?
n: Chartres Cathedral's west facade has the Royal Portal (about 1145–55), a triple portal of early Gothic sculpture that survived the 1194 fire. Source: UNESCO (Chartres Cathedral).

q: What is the gallery opening onto the nave at an upper level, below the clerestory?
n: The triforium is the arcaded wall passage or gallery opening onto the nave above the main arcade and below the clerestory. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: Which building is a splendid example of Early Gothic architecture?
n: Notre-Dame de Paris (begun 1163) is a prime example of Early Gothic, with sexpartite vaults and an early use of flying buttresses. Source: UNESCO (Paris, Banks of the Seine); Encyclopaedia Britannica.

q: Which Christopher Wren cathedral has a large central space under its dome for big congregations?
n: Christopher Wren's St. Paul's Cathedral, London (1675–1710) has a great domed central crossing that holds large congregations. Source: St. Paul's Cathedral official site; Encyclopaedia Britannica.

q: Which cathedral has the "Five Sisters" window?
n: York Minster's north transept has the Five Sisters window, five tall lancets of grey grisaille glass (about 1250). Source: York Minster official site.

q: How many years did it take to build the Notre Dame Cathedral in Paris?
n: Notre-Dame de Paris took about 182 years to build, from 1163 to about 1345. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Notre-Dame de Paris.

q: What is the tallest church in the world today?
n: Since its central Tower of Jesus Christ reached 162.91 m in 2025–26, the Sagrada Família has been the world's tallest church, passing Ulm Minster (161.53 m). Source: Sagrada Família official site; news reports 2025–26.

q: Which Gothic cathedral has the longest nave among Gothic churches?
n: Winchester Cathedral has the longest nave of any Gothic cathedral in Europe, and the cathedral is about 170 m long overall. Source: Winchester Cathedral official site.

q: Which cathedral has 176 stained-glass windows?
n: Chartres Cathedral keeps 176 stained-glass windows, most of them original 12th–13th-century glass. Source: UNESCO (Chartres Cathedral); Chartres Cathedral official site.

q: Which Romanesque cathedral has twin towers, a dome and apses at both ends?
n: Worms Cathedral is a double-ended Rhenish Romanesque church with apses and paired towers at both east and west ends and crossing domes. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Worms; Fletcher.

q: Which Italian Renaissance palace is built of brick and features quoining on the corners?
n: The Palazzo Farnese in Rome (Sangallo the Younger and Michelangelo) is a brick-faced Renaissance palace with rusticated stone quoins at the corners. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture; French Embassy in Italy (Palazzo Farnese).

q: What is the most influential building of the Byzantine period?
n: Hagia Sophia (532–537) is the most influential Byzantine building. Its vast dome on pendentives set the model for Byzantine churches and later Ottoman mosques. Source: UNESCO (Historic Areas of Istanbul); Encyclopaedia Britannica.

q: Cologne Cathedral, begun in 1248 and finished in 1880, took about how many years?
n: Cologne Cathedral was begun in 1248 and finished in 1880: 1880 − 1248 = 632 years. Source: UNESCO (Cologne Cathedral).

q: Which church is known for being a ‘Half Gothic, Half Renaissance’ architectural style?
n: Granada Cathedral (begun 1523) was started in Gothic by Enrique Egas and continued in Renaissance by Diego de Siloé, so it is half Gothic, half Renaissance. Source: Granada Cathedral official site; Encyclopaedia Britannica.

q: Which cathedral has the "Smiling Angel" sculpture at its doorway?
n: The "Smiling Angel" (L'Ange au Sourire, about 1240) is a statue at the west portal of Reims Cathedral. Source: UNESCO (Reims Cathedral); Encyclopaedia Britannica.

q: Which cathedral has two west towers of different designs?
n: Chartres has two dissimilar west towers: a plain 12th-century Romanesque south spire (about 105 m) and a Flamboyant Gothic north spire (about 113 m) added in 1507–13. Source: UNESCO (Chartres Cathedral).

q: Which church features twin towers of the same design but different heights?
n: Chartres's two west towers differ in both design and height: the Romanesque south spire is about 105 m and the Flamboyant north spire about 113 m. Source: UNESCO (Chartres Cathedral).

q: Which style name means "Roman-like"?
n: "Romanesque" means "Roman-like," for its round arches, barrel vaults and massive walls taken from Roman building. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Romanesque architecture.

q: Which vault was widely used in Romanesque churches to carry stone roofs?
n: Romanesque churches commonly used the barrel (tunnel) vault, and later groin vaults, to carry stone ceilings. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture; Fletcher.
